strengths: The paper offers a useful empirical perspective on multilingual visual supervision: captions originating in different languages may describe complementary concepts in the same image. This has practical relevance to dataset construction and synthetic caption generation.

The comparison uses shared images and matched caption-set sizes, addressing important confounders. Studying human Crossmodal captions across seven languages alongside LLaVA and Vertex outputs provides evidence beyond a single caption generator.

The Visual Genome evaluation supports an increase in grounded object coverage: Table 3 reports 9.6% coverage for three English Vertex captions versus 11.7% for English/French/Chinese captions. The separate study with 20 participants and 30 images also reports increased coverage from combining English and Japanese captions.

The translation assessment with 15 bilingual raters, supplementary embedding analysis, and held-out GIT fine-tuning experiments are meaningful attempts to validate the measurements and investigate downstream consequences. The manuscript also acknowledges limitations concerning language coverage and linguistic essentialism.
weaknesses: Material reporting inconsistencies undermine confidence in the quantitative evidence. The entire 6-by-6 LLaVA fine-tuning matrix in Table 14 exactly matches the corresponding Vertex entries in Table 4, including the multilingual row and column, despite representing different training sources. Table 2 also reports a Vertex monolingual attribute average of 1.98, although every constituent value lies between 1.59 and 1.86. These unresolved discrepancies affect the claimed independent replication and aggregate effect sizes.

The translation controls do not adequately validate expressive variation. Appendix 8.1 assesses factual preservation in model-generated captions, without including human XM captions or directly testing preservation of LIWC tone and authenticity. Near-chance source-language classification cannot establish that translation leaves the downstream measurements unbiased. Consequently, an important part of the claimed expressive variation remains difficult to separate from translation effects.

Larger scene-graph unions do not by themselves establish more correct visual information. Table 3 usefully measures grounded object recall, but the study does not quantify hallucination rates or validate the additional relations and attributes. Language-dependent caption length and generation diversity are also not characterized, limiting the interpretation of increased coverage as complementary visual selection.

The inference in Section 3.2 is unsupported: comparable diversity between multilingual outputs from one model and English outputs from several models does not rule out language-specific model behavior as the explanation. There is no justified bound requiring variation between language modes to be smaller than variation between models. The experiment contextualizes the magnitude of variation but does not identify its cause.

The fine-tuning results primarily demonstrate adaptation to caption-reference distributions. SPICE improvements against references originating in the training language remain compatible with learning annotation preferences and concept frequencies; they do not directly establish improved visual representations or robustness. The broader training benefits therefore remain plausible implications rather than demonstrated outcomes.

Reproducibility is incomplete: exact LLaVA and parser checkpoints, generation settings, concept-merging thresholds, and GIT training hyperparameters are not sufficiently specified. The principal coverage and fine-tuning tables also lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run results. Despite the worthwhile observational contribution, the unresolved numerical reliability and measurement-validity concerns currently favor weak rejection.
